title: My Tears Answered the Call of a Ruined Camp
intro: Ibn al-Iflili dates this poem of reconciliation with Sayf al-Dawla to Sha'ban 341 AH (952–953 CE). He relates that the prince received al-Mutanabbi again, dressed him in robes of honour and sent more gifts after him. A sword intrudes on a lovers’ embrace, then carries the poem from the abandoned camp to the man who gave it. Once in the prince’s presence, the poet can ask for pardon, a horse and a smile in the space of a single verse.

translation: My tears answered. Only the ruined camp had called.
It called, and they answered before the riders or the camels.
1.sharh: The deserted camp calls without a voice. Before a companion can speak or a camel give its cry of recognition, his eyes have answered.

translation: Among my dear companions I kept wiping them away.
They kept streaming amid excuses and reproaches.
2.sharh: He keeps wiping the tears away as fast as they flow. Al-Wahidi takes the two voices to be his companions’, some making allowances for him and some scolding him.

translation: I grieve at the distance. My tears astonish them.
They did this when only curtains stood between us.
3.sharh: His companions have forgotten how little it took to make him weep. Even when they lived in the same place, the slight barrier of a curtain was enough.

translation: Longing with some hope
of meeting is unlike longing with none.
4.sharh: He puts his old sorrow beside his present one. The curtain might be lifted. He can see no such end to the distance that now divides them.

translation: Whenever you visit the people of the woman you long to see,
their only gifts to you are swords and spears.
5.sharh: A visit to her means facing her whole clan. The word for honouring a guest with a present measures the distance between the welcome he wants and the one he would get.

translation: Estrangement is deadlier than the men I watch for.
I am drowning. Why should I fear getting wet?
6.sharh: He weighs the risk of visiting her against the grief he already lives with. To a drowning man, the threat of getting wet has come too late.

translation: How can every heart among her kin
hold what mine holds, when none of it has left me?
7.sharh: He finds a copy of his own love in every heart around her. He speaks as if something must have passed from him to them, yet he has parted with none of it.

translation: Other glances obey hers. She is their sovereign.
Her two eyes hold mighty sway over all eyes.
8.sharh: Her eyes govern what other eyes can do. Once a gaze meets hers it has lost the freedom to turn away, an interpretation al-Wahidi records from Ibn Furraja.

translation: The shy, companionable girls take after her
in their walk, and win their beauty by artifice.
9.sharh: The other women watch how she moves. A walk can be studied and copied, so that the very success of their imitation points back to the woman who needed no practice.

translation: I have tasted the hardship and the sweetness of my days.
Neither bitter sap nor honey is left to me.
10.sharh: Pleasure and hardship had quite distinct tastes while he was living them. Looking back, he finds that neither has left him so much as a drop of bitter sap or honey to keep.

translation: Youth showed me my soul in my own body.
Grey age showed me my soul in someone else’s.
11.sharh: The soul is still recognisable, the body carrying it almost a stranger. Ibn Furraja offered another reading in which the father sees his own young life again in a growing son.

translation: I have visited the girl of the camp by night, wearing
a companion neither cold to women nor amorous.
12.sharh: He has come by night with something slung over his shoulder. Calling it a companion makes us expect another man, though it can feel neither desire nor indifference.

translation: It lay between our collarbones. We kept pushing it aside.
It knew nothing of our complaints or kisses.
13.sharh: He has kept his sword on even in the embrace. Both lovers have to make room for it, an intimate witness incapable of understanding anything it witnesses.

translation: Next morning it went out marked with her perfume,
on its tassel, its scabbard and its leather covers.
14.sharh: Her scented cosmetic leaves a visible stain wherever the sword brushed her. Across strap, sheath and outer leather, the metal companion carries away a record of the meeting.

translation: I win renown only with its cutting edges,
or with a spearpoint on a straight, hard-jointed shaft.
15.sharh: The sword of the love scene is also the blade by which he expects to be known. The straight shaft and solid joints of the spear make a second measure of the weapons he trusts.

translation: The prince gave it to me from among his gifts.
It graced them, and among the robes he clothed me in mail.
16.sharh: At last the sword discloses its giver. The ruler’s gifts include both a robe of honour for court and armour to wear in battle, two ways of clothing the same guest.

translation: From Ali son of Abd Allah I learnt
to carry it. Who can match Abd Allah or Ali?
17.sharh: Ali is Sayf al-Dawla. The poet credits him with teaching him how to bear arms as well as equipping him, then pays the same honour to the prince and to his father.

translation: Giver of young women and sleek, long-limbed horses, of
bright, keen swords and slender, quivering spears.
18.sharh: The catalogue places enslaved young women beside gifts for a horseman. The Arabic article belonging to “bright swords” actually begins before the break between the two halves.

translation: All time and the face of the earth are too small for a king
who fills time itself, the plains and the mountains.
19.sharh: His deeds fill the historical record and his troops fill the landscape. The poet makes time feel as crowded as ground occupied by an army.

translation: We are glad, the Byzantines afraid,
the land is busy, the sea ashamed.
20.sharh: Four short, chiming phrases distribute his effects. His army keeps the land busy, while the sea, the usual measure of abundance, feels ashamed beside his generosity.

translation: He descends from Taghlib, who vanquish all others,
and from Adi, foes of cowardice and greed.
21.sharh: Each ancestral name supplies a piece of praise by its sound. Taghlib echoes the word for victors and Adi the word for enemies, here the sworn enemies of cowardice and meanness.

translation: To praise Abu al-Hayja’s son and prop your praise up
with pre-Islamic exploits is sheer ineptitude and folly.
22.sharh: Having just recited the prince’s ancestry, he questions what ancestral exploits can add. Al-Wahidi hears a thrust at another court poet who built his praise on pre-Islamic forebears.

translation: If only praise could do justice to his own deeds.
What room then for Kulayb and the men of old?
23.sharh: The most famous old chief of Taghlib makes a pointed test. Praise has more than it can do if it attends only to the ruler who is there to hear it.

translation: Take what you see and leave what you have heard about.
One sight of the full moon is enough to forget Saturn.
24.sharh: The present ruler can be seen for oneself, while the ancestors are known by report. Al-Nahari’s full moon puts the distant planet in the shade, as the sun does in the commentaries.

translation: You have found room enough for words here.
If you find a tongue that can speak, then speak.
25.sharh: There is no shortage of material before the poet. The hard thing to find is a tongue equal to it. The challenge can be heard as one he sets himself.

translation: The prince in whom mankind takes pride
is the finest sword in the hands of the finest state.
26.sharh: Sayf al-Dawla means “Sword of the State”. The title turns into a visible scene in which a state has two hands and a prince is the weapon they wield.

translation: Wishes fall dead before they reach his height.
Of nothing does he say, “I wish that were mine.”
27.sharh: Even his possible wishes have ground to cover before they catch up with what he has attained. The simple words of envy in the second half are words he never needs.

translation: Look, when the two swords meet in the battle dust,
how unlike they are in make and in their work.
28.sharh: One sword is a man, the other steel. For a moment the dust and the shared name put them on equal terms, just before the poet distinguishes their different powers.

translation: This one, drawn and ready for the blows of time,
made that one ready for the champion rider’s head.
29.sharh: Arabic points twice with the same word, “this”. The size of the task tells the swords apart. The man faces what time can bring, the blade a single opposing horseman.

translation: The Arabs fly from him with the dun sandgrouse,
the Byzantines fly from him with the partridges.
30.sharh: Each people flees in the company of a bird from its own terrain. The sandgrouse belongs to the open country and the partridge to the hills.

translation: What use is fleeing to the mountains from a lion
whom ostriches carry into the ibex’s stronghold?
31.sharh: The lion is the prince and the long-legged ostriches are his horses. Birds made for running on the plain carry him to a height where even an ibex should be safe.

translation: He crossed the passes to the country beyond Kharshana.
He left it, but the terror never left.
32.sharh: Prince and fear arrive together and part company at Kharshana. The same verb serves first for his departure and then for what his departure fails to remove.

translation: Whenever a young woman among them dreams,
she dreams only of captivity and the camel.
33.sharh: The raid enters a private room through a dream. The camel belongs to the captors, and the young woman imagines the animal that would carry her away from home.

translation: If you will accept tribute, they will give
all you ask. What would the one-eyed give for a squint?
34.sharh: He imagines tribute as the concession the defeated would most like to make. The proverb gives that difficult bargain a bodily measure, one injury seeming desirable to someone with a worse one.

translation: I called to your glory in my verse as the two set out,
“True and unborrowed, in lines as true as you.”
35.sharh: Glory and the poem bearing it are about to travel together. The same Arabic word can accuse a man of claiming another’s deeds or a poet of claiming another’s lines.

translation: “In east and west live people we love.
Seek them out, both of you, and be my finest messengers.
36.sharh: The addressees are still a pair. The instruction to visit his friends makes a poem’s passage from one listener to another into a journey the prince’s fame can share.

translation: Tell them that, surrounded by his bounty,
I look from horses to household attendants.”
37.sharh: His friends are to receive an eyewitness report of his good fortune. Moving his gaze from the horses to the household gives them something more definite than an assertion that he is well.

translation: Benefactor whom my lips have thanked,
the thanks come from your kindness, not from me.
38.sharh: He has just entrusted the prince’s reputation to his verse. Now he gives the prince credit even for the gratitude the verse expresses, since the original kindness called it forth.

translation: I slept only on the knowledge
that your judgement gives error no way in.
39.sharh: He lays his trust in the prince’s judgement beneath him like bedding. Al-Wahidi takes the sleep literally. Earlier readers heard an admission that trust had made the poet careless.

translation: Pardon, give, grant land, give a mount, raise me, console, restore.
Give more, welcome, smile, be gracious, draw me close, gladden, reward.
40.sharh: Seven imperatives fit into each half, from the gift of an estate to a smile of welcome. Al-Wahidi recounts that the prince wrote his responses beneath the petitions, word by word.

translation: Perhaps your displeasure will end in good.
Sickness has sometimes made a body well.
41.sharh: He hopes the breach will leave the relationship the sounder for having been mended. A body that gains health through illness gives that reversal its unexpected shape.

translation: Neither I nor anyone else has heard of anyone in power
readier than you to defend a man against a lie.
42.sharh: The ruler who hears a malicious report has the power to act on it. What reassures the poet is his readiness to use that power in defence of the person accused.

translation: Your forbearance comes without effort.
Painted kohl cannot match eyes dark by nature.
43.sharh: Arabic distinguishes the act of applying kohl from the naturally dark line around an eye. The prince’s restraint belongs to him as completely as a feature he was born with.

translation: People’s talk never turned you from generosity.
Who can bar the way of a cloud heavy with rain?
44.sharh: The slanderers have already failed to make him punish anyone. They are equally powerless to stop his gifts, as if talk could hold back an advancing rain cloud.

translation: You give without reminders or bitterness,
without delays, promises or a pang of regret.
45.sharh: A gift can cost its recipient time, embarrassment and the knowledge that the giver wishes it back. The successive negatives free the recipient from each of those burdens.

translation: You are brave when a horse can tread
only on mail, torn limbs and the heads of the fallen,
46.sharh: He singles out the moment when there is no bare earth left for a horse’s hoof. The view from ground level conveys what it costs to stand firm there.

translation: when shafts beat one another back, blow for blow,
as if arguing over the men’s very lives.
47.sharh: A thrust receives an answer, and that answer another. The spears seem to conduct a dispute of their own over whether the men who wield them will live.

translation: May you always strike those who oppose you from whatever side,
with victory swift to come and the end of life slow.
48.sharh: The final blessing gives time two different speeds. Victory is to reach the prince without delay, while the end that would cut his victories short keeps its distance.

1.1.6.head: طَلَل
1.1.6.meaning: The still-visible remains of an abandoned dwelling or campsite.

2.1.4.head: كَفكَفَ
2.1.4.meaning: To hold back repeatedly, here to keep wiping away tears.

2.2.5.head: عَذَل
2.2.5.meaning: Reproach, especially of a lover who gives way to grief.

3.1.2.meaning: Distance and separation from loved ones.

3.2.2.head: كانَ
3.2.2.meaning: “It was”, referring to his tear. Al-Wahidi also gives “I was”, making the poet himself the subject.

3.2.6.head: كِلَل
3.2.6.meaning: Light curtains around an enclosure or litter.

4.1.2.head: صَبابَة
4.1.2.meaning: Tender yearning, especially for an absent beloved.

5.2.2.head: أَتحَفَ
5.2.2.meaning: To honour a guest with a gift.

5.2.4-5.head: البيض وَالأَسَل
5.2.4-5.meaning: “The white ones and spearpoints”: swords and spears.

6.1.4.meaning: “Than the people whom”, here the men he watches warily. Ibn al-Iflili gives this personal form. Al-Wahidi explains the comparison in terms of the harm he fears.

7.1.6.head: عَشيرَة
7.1.6.meaning: A person’s close kin or clan.

8.1.2.head: لَحظ
8.1.2.meaning: A glance, particularly a sidelong one.

8.2.1.head: مُقلَة
8.2.1.meaning: The eye, particularly the eyeball seen in its entirety.

9.1.3.head: آنِسَة
9.1.3.meaning: A woman whose company puts a visitor at ease.

10.2.4.head: صاب
10.2.4.meaning: Sab, a plant whose sap is proverbial for bitterness.

11.2.6.head: بَدَل
11.2.6.meaning: A substitute or other self, here the changed body of old age.

12.2.3.head: عِزهاة
12.2.3.meaning: A man indifferent to women and amorous pursuits.

13.1.4.head: دَفَّعَ
13.1.4.meaning: To keep nudging aside. Al-Wahidi reads a form suggesting that the lovers struggle against the sword.

14.1.5.head: رَدع
14.1.5.meaning: A smear of coloured perfume, especially saffron.

14.2.2.head: ذُؤابَة
14.2.2.meaning: A pendant strap or tassel on a sword hilt.

14.2.3-4.head: الجَفن وَالخِلَل
14.2.3-4.meaning: “Sheath and coverings”: the scabbard and the outer sleeves around it.

15.1.6.head: مَضرِب
15.1.6.meaning: The striking or cutting part of a blade.

15.2.4-5.head: أَصَمّ الكَعب
15.2.4-5.meaning: “Solid at the joints”: a strong spear shaft with firm nodes.

16.1.5.meaning: “From among.” The two commentary texts put the sword “among his gifts” with fi.

17.1.2-5.head: عَلِيّ بن عَبد اللَّه
17.1.2-5.meaning: Ali ibn Abd Allah is Sayf al-Dawla, Hamdanid ruler of Aleppo.

18.1.2.head: كَواعِب
18.1.2.meaning: Young women in early maturity, here women given in slavery.

18.1.3-4.head: الجُرد السَّلاهِب
18.1.3-4.meaning: “Sleek, tall ones”: long-limbed horses with short coats.

18.2.3-4.head: العَسّالَة الذُّبُل
18.2.3-4.meaning: “Quivering, slender ones” describes spear shafts that flex when shaken. The ending is hard to hear here. The written l is the poem’s rhyme.

21.1.2.head: تَغلِب
21.1.2.meaning: Taghlib, the tribe of Rabi'a to which the Hamdanids traced their descent.

21.2.2.head: عَدِيّ
21.2.2.meaning: Adi, an ancestor in the Taghlib line. His name echoes the following word for enemies.

22.1.3-4.head: أَبو الهَيجاء
22.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Hayja, the title of Sayf al-Dawla’s father.

22.1.5.head: أَنجَدَ
22.1.5.meaning: To help or reinforce, here to prop up a eulogy.

23.2.2.head: كُلَيب
23.2.2.meaning: Kulayb ibn Rabi'a, a celebrated pre-Islamic leader of Taghlib.

24.2.3.head: بَدر
24.2.3.meaning: The full moon. Al-Nahari sings of the moon. Al-Wahidi names the sun, and Ibn al-Iflili also explains the image as sunlight outshining Saturn.

24.2.7.head: زُحَل
24.2.7.meaning: Saturn, standing for a far and comparatively faint light.

25.1.3.head: مَكان
25.1.3.meaning: Room or scope for speech. Ibn al-Iflili has this wording. Al-Wahidi reads majal, the field open to a poet.

26.1.2.head: هُمام
26.1.2.meaning: A man of high resolve, a lord or champion.

27.1.3.meaning: Struck down, like the fallen on a battlefield.

28.1.6.head: رَهَج
28.1.6.meaning: Dust raised by troops or horses in battle.

29.1.5.head: مُنصَلِت
29.1.5.meaning: Drawn from the scabbard, flashing into action.

30.1.4.head: كُدرِيّ
30.1.4.meaning: Dun-coloured sandgrouse of the open country.

30.2.5.head: حَجَل
30.2.5.meaning: Partridges, here identified with mountain country.

31.2.5.head: مَعقِل
31.2.5.meaning: A stronghold or secure place of refuge.

31.2.6.head: وَعَل
31.2.6.meaning: An ibex, proverbial for reaching the highest crags.

32.1.2.head: الدُّروب
32.1.2.meaning: The mountain passes across the frontier.

32.1.6.head: خَرشَنَة
32.1.6.meaning: Kharshana, the Byzantine frontier district and fortress known as Charsianon.

33.2.3.head: سَبي
33.2.3.meaning: Capture of people in war, often into enslavement.

34.1.6.head: جِزى
34.1.6.meaning: Tribute paid under an agreement of protection.

34.2.4-5.head: لِلعورِ بِالحَوَل
34.2.4-5.meaning: “A squint for the one-eyed”: a proverb about being glad to exchange a worse affliction for a lesser one.

35.1.6.head: صَدَرَ
35.1.6.meaning: To set out again after a visit, here with a dual subject.

35.2.3.head: اِنتَحَلَ
35.2.3.meaning: To claim falsely as one’s own, including another poet’s verse.

38.2.2-3.head: مِن قِبَل
38.2.2-3.meaning: “From the side of”: by reason of.

40.1.1.meaning: Pardon a lapse or release someone from its consequences.

40.1.3.head: أَقطِع
40.1.3.meaning: Grant an estate or parcel of land.

40.1.4.meaning: Furnish the petitioner with a mount.

40.1.5-6.meaning: “Raise, console”: restore my standing and dispel my sorrow.

40.2.2-3.meaning: “Welcome, smile”: receive me eagerly and with a bright face.

40.2.6.meaning: Gladden me. Al-Wahidi relates a courtly pun in which the poet claims to have asked for a concubine.

42.1.1.head: لا
42.1.1.meaning: “I have never heard.” Al-Nahari and the Berlin edition of al-Wahidi repeat the negative before “anyone else”. Ibn al-Iflili opens with wa-ma.

42.2.1.head: أَذَبّ
42.2.1.meaning: Readier to repel an attack or accusation.

43.2.5.head: كَحَل
43.2.5.meaning: A natural darkness of the eyelids, as distinct from applied kohl.

44.2.4.head: عارِض
44.2.4.meaning: A bank of cloud coming into sight.

45.2.6.head: مَذَل
45.2.6.meaning: Vexation or restlessness at what one has had to give.

46.1.7.head: فَرَس
46.1.7.meaning: A horse. The onset sounds close to th in the recording. Both commentators identify the horse as the animal treading the battlefield.

48.1.6-7.head: عَن عُرُض
48.1.6-7.meaning: “From whatever quarter”: taking opponents as they come.
